author: blu
body: The chain walk. X509 said what a certificate IS; this chapter says whether to believe it. The two are kept apart on purpose: a parser that also decides trust tends to decide it by accident, in a branch nobody meant as a policy.

author: blu
body: A verdict is a variant and never a Boolean. "False" tells a caller that something is wrong and nothing about what, which means the caller cannot log it, cannot alert on it, and cannot tell an expired certificate (a clock problem, probably benign) from a bad signature (an attack, never benign). Every rejection below names itself.

author: blu
body: This chapter has NO CLOCK. The current time is a parameter, because a library that reaches for a clock cannot be tested at an interesting instant and cannot run where there is no clock -- and on bare metal there often is not one. The caller supplies the time; the caller is where the clock lives.

author: blu
body: A time field that is not digits is not a time. A parser that shrugs at this is a parser that will compare garbage and get an answer.

author: blu
body: notBefore <= now <= notAfter. Both ends, and the failures are told apart: a certificate that is not valid yet is usually a clock that is wrong, and one that has expired is usually a certificate that has expired.

author: blu
body: Four combinations of curve and digest, four named functions and no flag between them. A P-384 root signed under SHA-384 is the case that matters; P-384 under SHA-256 is legal and is wired rather than left to fall through to a False that would read as a refusal on policy.
